\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{موجة} \ar{حر} (mawjat ḥarr)}{موجة حر (mawjat ḥarr)}]{\ar{موجة} \ar{حر} (mawjat ḥarr) — a heatwave}

\label{lesson:AR-C484-mawjat-harr}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for frost, then the Arabic for to get cold.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{موجة} \ar{حر}}
\textbf{\ar{موجة} \ar{حر}} — \emph{mawjat ḥarr} — \textquotedblleft{}a heatwave\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{وصلت} \ar{موجة} \ar{حر} \ar{إلى} \ar{المدينة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{waṣalat mawjat ḥarr ilā al-madīna.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
A heatwave reached the city.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{موجة} \ar{حر}} (\emph{mawjat ḥarr}) is built from two native Arabic words: \emph{mawja}, \textquotedblleft{}a wave\textquotedblright{}, on the root \emph{m-w-j} (Lane), and \emph{ḥarr}, \textquotedblleft{}heat\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{ḥ-r-r} (Lane).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for getting around.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mawjat ḥarr}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mawjat ḥarr}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{waṣalat mawjat ḥarr ilā al-madīna.} — A heatwave reached the city.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for frost, then the Arabic for to get cold, then say \emph{mawjat ḥarr} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{موجة} \ar{حر} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A heatwave\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{خانق} (khāniq)}{خانق (khāniq)}]{\ar{خانق} (khāniq) — stifling; suffocating}

\label{lesson:AR-C484-khaniq}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to get cold, then the Arabic for a heatwave.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{خانق}}
\textbf{\ar{خانق}} — \emph{khāniq} — \textquotedblleft{}stifling; suffocating\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{كان} \ar{الحر} \ar{خانقا} \ar{في} \ar{الحافلة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kāna al-ḥarr khāniqan fī al-ḥāfila.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The heat was stifling on the bus.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{خانق}} (\emph{khāniq}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{kh-n-q}, \textquotedblleft{}to strangle\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is the active participle, \textquotedblleft{}choking\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for getting around.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to get cold, then the Arabic for a heatwave, then say \emph{khāniq} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{رطوبة} (ruṭūba)}{رطوبة (ruṭūba)}]{\ar{رطوبة} (ruṭūba) — humidity; moisture}

\label{lesson:AR-C484-rutuba}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a heatwave, then the Arabic for stifling.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{رطوبة}}
\textbf{\ar{رطوبة}} — \emph{ruṭūba} — \textquotedblleft{}humidity; moisture\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{الرطوبة} \ar{على} \ar{الساحل} \ar{مرتفعة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ar-ruṭūba ʿalā as-sāḥil murtafiʿa.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The humidity on the coast is high.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{رطوبة}} (\emph{ruṭūba}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{r-ṭ-b}, \textquotedblleft{}to be moist\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is the noun beside \emph{raṭb}, \textquotedblleft{}humid\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for getting around.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{جفاف} (jafāf)}{جفاف (jafāf)}]{\ar{جفاف} (jafāf) — drought; dryness}

\label{lesson:AR-C484-jafaf}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for stifling, then the Arabic for humidity.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{جفاف}}
\textbf{\ar{جفاف}} — \emph{jafāf} — \textquotedblleft{}drought; dryness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{ذبل} \ar{الزرع} \ar{بسبب} \ar{الجفاف}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{dhabala az-zarʿ bi-sabab al-jafāf.}

\begin{quote}

\textbf{\ar{جفاف}} (\emph{jafāf}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{j-f-f}, \textquotedblleft{}to be dry\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is the noun beside \emph{jāff}, \textquotedblleft{}dry\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for getting around.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{تبخر} (tabakhkhara)}{تبخر (tabakhkhara)}]{\ar{تبخر} (tabakhkhara) — to evaporate}

\label{lesson:AR-C484-tabakhkhara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for humidity, then the Arabic for drought.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{تبخر}}
\textbf{\ar{تبخر}} — \emph{tabakhkhara} — \textquotedblleft{}to evaporate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{تبخر} \ar{الماء} \ar{في} \ar{الشمس}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tabakhkhara al-māʾ fī ash-shams.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The water evaporated in the sun.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يتبخر}, \emph{yatabakhkhar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{تبخر}} (\emph{tabakhkhara}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{b-kh-r}, \textquotedblleft{}vapour, steam\textquotedblright{} (Lane). It is Form V, \textquotedblleft{}to turn to vapour\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for getting around.
\end{grammarlens}

\end{itemize}
